# The Silent World Cup Winners are the Companies Normalizing Surveillance

Spain fans gather for a rally on the eve of the World Cup final soccer match in New York's Times Square, Saturday, July 18, 2026 (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)

The 2026 World Cup ends this Sunday with a historic match between Argentina and Spain. Which team will secure its place in the history books remains to be seen. But after the stadium lights go out, a different kind of legacy will remain. The US, Mexico, and Canada have built up an ecosystem of surveillance technologies under the justification of ensuring the safety and security of the event. In doing so, they follow in the footsteps of past events like the Men’s World Cup in South Africa, Brazil and Qatar, and the Olympic and Paralympic games in Paris.

This week, Ranking Digital Rights (RDR) released an [in-depth investigation](https://rankingdigitalrights.org/2026/07/14/no-fair-play-mapping-the-2026-world-cup-surveillance-stack/) into the companies supporting the expansion of surveillance tools and policing capabilities in the 16 host cities of the 2026 World Cup. We found that at least 21 companies helped build or enhance the surveillance structures used to monitor, track, and profile fans, visitors, and locals. These vendors provide products and services that we classify into a five-layer stack: data harvesting at scale, predictive policing, communications interception, data integration and command centers, and aerial surveillance.

What exactly is the “surveillance stack”? We use the framing proposed by New York University law professor [Vincent M. Southerland](https://www.uclalawreview.org/the-masters-tools-and-a-mission-using-community-control-and-oversight-laws-to-resist-and-abolish-police-surveillance-technologies/): the surveillance stack is a set of technologies that are used to “surveil indiscriminately, and which are rarely governed by a warrant requirement or any of the traditional legal oversight mechanisms,” guiding decisions about “who to police, where to police, how to police, and when to police.” This definition encompasses AI-powered systems that process and analyze large amounts of data to monitor, track, and profile individuals and communities.

## Surveillance and human rights in the 2026 World Cup

In July 2025, the US Department of Homeland Security introduced a [new grant](https://www.fema.gov/fifa-world-cup-2026) under the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), awarding $846 million to strengthen security operations and protect against drone threats in the eleven US host cities. Detailed breakdowns of how these funds were used and which companies benefited are elusive, but we know that Atlanta, Boston, and Dallas allocated part of their grants to expanding drone units, camera networks, and real-time police intelligence capabilities. Some of the companies that scored new contracts through these and other grants include longstanding government providers like weapons tech manufacturer Axon and technology consulting giant Booz Allen Hamilton.

In spite of this new influx of cash, the tournament’s host cities failed to establish strong due diligence processes, risk mitigation, and remedy mechanisms to consider the human rights impacts and harms associated with surveillance products and services. In 2026, for the first time in the history of the tournament, FIFA required that each host city develop its own human rights action plan. But by April of this year, [only four of the 16 locations](https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/04/10/world-cup-2-months-out-fifa-and-host-cities-sideline-rights) had published theirs. As RDR’s report shows, by the time the tournament started, three cities (Seattle, Mexico City, and Monterrey) had yet to make their plans public. (Monterrey [published](https://www.instagram.com/p/DZF_WVeEWdY/) its human rights action plan on June 2, but it was only available as an Instagram Story.)

The majority of the action plans did not fully consider the human rights impacts that could arise from the extensive use of technology, especially surveillance and data protection risks. Only [Boston,](https://web.archive.org/web/20260612023456/https://bostonfwc26.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Human-Rights-Action-Plan_FWCBOSTON-1.pdf) [Toronto](https://web.archive.org/web/20260609092208/https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/8f02-FWC26-Toronto-HRAPFinal.pdf), and [Vancouver](https://web.archive.org/web/20260525220633/https://media.vancouverfwc26.ca//website-assets/community-hub/Human%20Rights/Host%20City%20Human%20Rights%20Action%20Plan.pdf) had dedicated sections with considerations for the right to privacy. Vancouver was the only city that established a clear and explicit plan for when the technology used during the World Cup, namely the expanded CCTV infrastructure, would be dismantled.

The omissions in the host cities’ human rights action plans are the latest chapter in the history of opacity and lack of accountability over surveillance and policing, particularly in the US. Companies like Flock Safety, Clearview AI, and Palantir are already established providers of tech used by law enforcement agencies at various jurisdictional levels. But the municipal action plans display a complete lack of recognition for how existing surveillance infrastructure could impact the rights of locals and fans. For example, in Atlanta, one of the [most surveilled cities](https://www.acluga.org/issues/speech-and-privacy/) in the US, law enforcement has usedFlock Safety‘s license plate reader cameras to [conduct](https://www.ajc.com/opinion/2026/04/atlanta-surveillance-is-more-vast-than-you-think-time-for-stronger-oversight/) [immigration lookups](https://www.404media.co/ice-taps-into-nationwide-ai-enabled-camera-network-data-shows/) [on behalf](https://atlpresscollective.com/2025/06/03/flock-metro-atlanta-ice/) of ICE. In Kansas City, the municipal Transportation Authority [plans to install](https://www.kctv5.com/2026/06/18/kansas-citys-push-facial-recognition-public-buses-ignites-debate-over-security-privacy/) cameras with facial recognition in public buses after delaying their deployment during the tournament, prompting fears among civil rights advocates that the technology will continue to operate indefinitely.

A FIFA World Cup Trophy visual is displayed against the Manhattan skyline during the FIFA Drone show in New York/New Jersey at Liberty State Park on July 17, 2026 in Jersey City, New Jersey. (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images)

## From the stadiums to the streets and the borders

[Our research found](https://rankingdigitalrights.org/2026/07/14/no-fair-play-mapping-the-2026-world-cup-surveillance-stack/) that at least 15 companies entered into new agreements or renewed existing partnerships with the 16 host cities to provide surveillance tools around the World Cup. But these vendors are part of a broader stack of corporate actors and monitoring tools that are already woven into the urban infrastructure.

#### Our content delivered to your inbox.

#### Thank you!

Lenovo, FIFA’s official technology partner, had a prominent role in building the digital infrastructure for the venues. The company created an [Intelligent Command Center](https://news.lenovo.com/building-an-intelligent-command-center-for-fifa-world-cup-2026/)and[3D Digital Twins](https://technologymagazine.com/news/the-technology-behind-the-fifa-world-cup-2026)—detailed virtual maps of all 16 stadiums— that ran crowd pattern identification and predictive analytics to facilitate safety and security interventions. Facial recognition technology continues to be deployed in stadiums, used for access control and purchases in food stalls. At least two venues in this World Cup made use of this technology: Boston's Gillette Stadium, which partnered with [NWN](https://nwn.ai/news-room/news/wcvb-channel5-nwn-kraft/), and Atlanta's Mercedes-Benz Stadium, which partnered with [Wicket](https://www.wicketsoft.com/case-studies/mbs/). These stadiums add to a [growing list](https://slate.com/technology/2023/03/madison-square-garden-facial-recognition-stadiums-list.html) of entertainment sites that are deploying and normalizing the use of facial recognition in public spaces. World Cup surveillance also [extends to the skies](https://epic.org/issues/surveillance-oversight/aerial-surveillance/) through companies like Fortem Technologies and Ondas Inc., which received contracts to deploy drone and counter-drone systems across multiple cities.

Once fans exit the stadiums, they encounter the increasingly pervasive tech in the streets.

Companies like Flock Safety and Motorola are behind the [massive surge](https://web.archive.org/web/20260704110449/https://www.wired.com/story/us-world-cup-2026-alpr-camera-stadiums/) of automated license plate readers (ALPRs), with volunteer mapping project [DeFlock](https://deflock.org/) logging more than 650 devices in Atlanta, Los Angeles, Houston, and New Jersey. The Houston City Council [purchased](https://abc13.com/post/privacy-concerns-raised-houston-approves-second-ai-traffic-camera-purchase/19095721/) access to MoboTrex (Derq)’s AI-powered video detection systemto track vehicles and pedestrians; Nexera’s KeepZone AI provided a threat detection system to Mexican authorities; and Peregrine’s integrated public safety platforms were [in place](https://web.archive.org/web/20260712030431/https://www.nbcnews.com/video/how-law-enforcement-is-utilizing-ai-to-sort-through-data-264056389926) across all 11 host cities in the US. Seguritech, one of the [major government contractors](https://poplab.mx/especiales/seguritech-la-rentabilidad-del-miedo-camaras-videovigilancia-mexico/contratos-seguritech/) in Mexico, [advertised its role](https://www.facebook.com/GpoSeguritech/videos/el-evento-deportivo-del-a%C3%B1o-empieza-en-4-d%C3%ADas-sabes-qui%C3%A9n-lo-protege48-seleccion/2773855449680356/) in the 2026 World Cup in its social media profiles, claiming to implement a security operation that ranges from CCTV, analytics, drones, and cybersecurity services, all coordinated into a critical mission tech system.

All the technologies described above compound human rights impacts, from the right to privacy, to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. Data harvesting and identification tools, as well as data systems like the ones Clearview AI and Axon Enterprise deploy, exacerbate over-policing bias towards minorities and incur high [error rates](https://spectrum.ieee.org/facial-recognition-gone-wrong). Their use in public spaces also creates an environment of fear that [stifles political freedom](https://www.ohchr.org/en/press-releases/2026/04/un-experts-safeguard-human-freedoms-systematic-digital-interference) and has already been linked with numerous [wrongful arrests](https://www.vice.com/en/article/faulty-facial-recognition-led-to-his-arrestnow-hes-suing/). Likewise, predictive policing systems are trained with [historically biased datasets](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2212473X26000234) and risk increasing the targeting of marginalized communities. Data integration and command centers like Palantir’s Gotham platform create extensive [capacity for mass profiling](https://theconversation.com/when-the-government-can-see-everything-how-one-company-palantir-is-mapping-the-nations-data-263178) thanks to the consolidation of multiple data flows into a single source of information. Aerial surveillance with drone and counter-drone systems, like those of Robin Radar Systemsand Fortem Technologies, support [indiscriminate surveillance](https://web.archive.org/web/20260501200424/https://epic.org/issues/surveillance-oversight/aerial-surveillance/) and carry exposure...

## Reclaiming the game—and our neighborhoods

As video surveillance, facial recognition technology, and behavioral analytics [continue](https://privacyinternational.org/long-read/5759/moving-goalposts-football-facial-recognition-and-expansion-surveillance) to [proliferate](https://www.tedic.org/lanzamos-una-investigacion-sobre-vigilancia-biometrica-y-reconocimiento-facial-en-estadios-de-paraguay/), tech-facilitated hyper-surveillance quietly becomes the norm at mega-events and remains in place long after they end. The spread of surveillance technologies is known to lead to [chilling effects](https://scholarship.law.umn.edu/minnlrev/vol106/iss3/6/), introducing behavioral changes in people who know, or even just have a suspicion that they are being watched. Ultimately, this can erode speech and push behavior toward social conformity, restricting expression that is deemed unacceptable. But the technology and its direct effects belie the far broader problem of [deep](http://pbs.org/newshour/politics/poll-nearly-two-thirds-of-americans-say-ice-has-gone-too-far-in-immigration-crackdown) societal [distrust](https://www.pewresearch.org/race-and-ethnicity/2025/05/07/views-of-race-policing-and-black-lives-matter-in-the-5-years-since-george-floyds-killing/#how-americans-views-of-police-conduct-have-changed) toward law enforcement institutions and the systematic impunity they enjoy after committing egregious human rights violations. Companies and governments must respect people’s rights and freedoms, and due diligence mechanisms must be in place to protect them.

Together, activists and civil society are pushing back against the widespread use and abuse of surveillance at mega-events around the world. In doing so, they are also taking a stand against the failures of the global socioeconomic order that produced this reality, from labor abuse to housing exploitation. [Local](https://www.noiceinthecup.us/), [national](https://wagingnonviolence.org/2026/06/no-ice-in-the-world-cup/), and [international](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/05/16/fifa-publish-robust-rights-framework-2026-world-cup) coalitions are taking a stand. But other clusters of resistance are highly decentralized: individual, anonymous [hackers](https://cybernews.com/privacy/ice-surveillance-tech-hackers-push-back/)and [digital rights organizations](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/03/meet-rayhunter-new-open-source-tool-eff-detect-cellular-spying) are increasingly sharing creative ways for people to circumvent everyday surveillance.

The links between powerful tech companies and the FIFA World Cup’s global sociopolitical influence deserve far more scrutiny than they have received. In the face of this power, the momentum built by those resisting AI-powered surveillance will not end with the final whistle. Looking forward to the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games, communities are coming together and learning from [previous Olympic Games](https://prismreports.org/2024/09/05/los-angeles-olympics-protests/) to build campaigns calling on companies, governments and other stakeholders to invest in people instead of a permaculture of surveillance.

# 在 2026 世界盃的背後：被監視的世界

支持 2026 年世界盃擴展監控工具和執法能力的公司的身影，將成為這次歷史性賽事留下的另一種傳承。美國、墨西哥與加拿大為了確保賽事安全而建立了一個以監控為基礎的生態系統。在過去的男子足球世界盃（南非、巴西及卡達）、巴黎奧運與帕運會中，我們也曾見證過類似的發展。

本週，隱私權排名組織 (Ranking Digital Rights, RDR) 發布了一項深入調查 [1](https://rankingdigitalrights.org/2026/07/14/no-fair-play-mapping-the-2026-world-cup-surveillance-stack/)，揭露了在 2026 年世界盃 16 個主辦城市中，協助建構或強化監控結構的公司。我們發現至少有 21 家公司參與其中，這些公司提供產品與服務，幫助建立並提升用於監控、追蹤及描繪球迷、遊客和當地居民的監控系統。

這些供應商提供的項目被歸類為一個五層堆疊：大規模資料收集、預測性執法、通訊攔截、數據整合以及指揮中心，最後是空中監視。

那麼，「監控堆疊」到底是什麼？我們採用了紐約大學法律教授 [Vincent M. Southerland](https://www.uclalawreview.org/the-masters-tools-and-a-mission-using-community-control-and-oversight-laws-to-resist-and-abolish-police-surveillance-technologies/) 提出的框架：監控堆疊是一套用於「無差別監視」且「罕見受搜索令或傳統法律監督機制約束」的技術集合，指引著關於「何人應被執法、何地執法、如何執法以及何時執法」的決策。這包括 AI 驅動系統處理與分析大量資料以監控、追蹤並描繪個人及社區的能力。

#### 感謝！

作為 FIFA 的官方科技合作夥伴，聯想（Lenovo）在為場館建設數位基礎設施方面發揮了重要作用。該公司建立了 [智慧指揮中心](https://news.lenovo.com/building-an-intelligent-command-center-for-fifa-world-cup-2026/)和 [3D 虛擬雙胞胎](https://technologymagazine.com/news/the-technology-behind-the-fifa-world-cup-2026)（為所有 16 個體育場製作的詳細虛擬地圖，用於人流識別和預測分析，以促進安全與安保措施）。臉部辨識技術在體育場中持續被使用，用於入口管制和攤販消費。在本屆世界盃中，至少有兩個場館使用了這項技術：波士頓的蓋特利體育場（Gillette Stadium），該場館與 [NWN](https://nwn.ai/news-room/news/wcvb-channel5-nwn-kraft/）合作；以及亞特蘭大的大都會銀行體育場（Mercedes-Benz Stadium），該場館則與 [Wicket](https://www.wicketsoft.com/case-studies/mbs/) 合作。這些體育場是 [日益增長的清單](https://slate.com/technology/2023/03/madison-square-garden-facial-recognition-stadiums-list.html)的一部分，娛樂場所正將臉部辨識技術的應用與使用普及化。世界盃的監控還 [延伸至天空](https://epic.org/issues/surveillance-oversight/aerial-surveillance/)，涉及 Fortem Technologies 和 Ondas Inc. 等公司，這些公司獲得了在多個城市部署無人機和反無人機系統的合約。

當粉絲離開體育場後，他們會遇到街頭日益普遍的科技。

公司如 Flock Safety 和 Motorola，正推動自動化車牌辨識系統（ALPRs）的[大規模增長](https://web.archive.org/web/20260704110449/https://www.wired.com/story/us-world-cup-2026-alpr-camera-stadiums/)，志工製作計畫[DeFlock](https://deflock.org/)已在亞特蘭大、洛杉磯、休士頓和新澤西州記錄超過 650 個裝置。休士頓市議會[購買了](https://abc13.com/post/privacy-concerns-raised-houston-approves-second-ai-traffic-camera-purchase/19095721/)對 MoboTrex（Derq）的 AI 驅動影片偵測系統存取權限，以追蹤車輛和行人和行人；Nexera 的 KeepZone AI 為墨西哥當局提供了威脅偵測系統；以及 Peregrine 的整合公共安全平台已[全面上線](https://web.archive.org/web/20260712030431/https://www.nbcnews.com/video/how-law-enforcement-is-utilizing-ai-to-sort-through-data-264056389926)於美國 11 個主辦城市的全部公共安全平台。Seguritech，作為墨西哥主要的政府承包商之一[廣告了](https://www.facebook.com/GpoSeguritech/videos/el-evento-deportivo-del-a%C3%B1o-empieza-en-4-d%C3%ADas-sabes-qui%C3%A9n-lo-protege48-seleccion/2773855449680356/)在 2026 世界盃的社群媒體檔案，聲稱實施一項從 CCTV、分析、無人機到網路安全服務的綜合維安任務系統。

技術發展如上所述，對人權產生複合性影響，從隱私權到言論自由以及和平集會的權利。資料收集與辨識工具，例如 Clearview AI 和 Axon Enterprise 部署的系統，加劇了針對少數族裔的過度執法偏見，並導致高 [錯誤率](https://spectrum.ieee.org/facial-recognition-gone-wrong)。在公共空間的使用也創造了一種恐懼氛圍，[抑制政治自由](https://www.ohchr.org/en/press-releases/2026/04/un-experts-safeguard-human-freedoms-systematic-digital-interference)，並與眾多 [錯誤逮捕](https://www.vice.com/en/article/faulty-facial-recognition-led-to-his-arrestnow-hes-suing/)案例相關聯。同樣地，預測性執法系統以[歷史上偏頗的資料集](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2212473X26000234)為基礎進行訓練，並可能增加對邊緣化社群的針對性。整合與指揮中心如 Palantir 的 Gotham 平台創造了廣泛的 [大規模側寫能力](https://theconversation.com/when-the-government-can-see-everything-how-one-company-palantir-is-mapping-the-nations-data-263178)，因為將多個資料流整合為單一資訊來源。無人機與反無人機系統，如 Robin Radar Systems 和 Fortem Technologies 的技術，支持 [不分青紅皂白監控](https://web.archive.org/web/20260501200424/https://epic.org/issues/surveillance-oversight/aerial-surveillance/)並帶來[暴露風險](https)。

As video surveillance, facial recognition technology, and behavioral analytics [continue](https://privacyinternational.org/long-read/5759/moving-goalposts-football-facial-recognition-and-expansion-surveillance) to [proliferate](https://www.tedic.org/lanzamos-una-investigacion-sobre-vigilancia-biometrica-y-reconocimiento-facial-en-estadios-de-paraguay/), tech-facilitated hyper-surveillance quietly becomes the norm at mega-events and remains in place long after they end. The spread of surveillance technologies is known to lead to [chilling effects](https://scholarship.law.umn.edu/minnlrev/vol106/iss3/6/), introducing behavioral changes in people who know, or even just have a suspicion that they are being watched. Ultimately, this can erode speech and push behavior toward social conformity, restricting expression that is deemed unacceptable. But the technology and its direct effects belie the far broader problem of [deep](http://pbs.org/newshour/politics/poll-nearly-two-thirds-of-americans-say-ice-has-gone-too-far-in-immigration-crackdown) societal [distrust](https://www.pewresearch.org/race-and-ethnicity/2025/05/07/views-of-race-policing-and-black-lives-matter-in-the-5-years-since-george-floyds-killing/#how-americans-views-of-police-conduct-have-changed) toward law enforcement institutions and the systematic impunity they enjoy after committing egregious human rights violations. Companies and governments must respect people’s rights and freedoms, and due diligence mechanisms must be in place to protect them。

一起，活動人士和公民社會正努力阻止在世界各地的重大活動中監控的使用與濫用。在此過程中，他們也在抵制導致這一現實的全球社會經濟秩序的失敗，從勞工剝削到居住權剝奪。 [Local](https://www.noiceinthecup.us/)、[national](https://wagingnonviolence.org/2026/06/no-ice-in-the-world-cup/), 和 [international](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/05/16/fifa-publish-robust-rights-framework-2026-world-cup) 的聯盟正在採取立場。但其他分散的抵抗群體則高度去中心化：個人、匿名的 [hackers](https://cybernews.com/privacy/ice-surveillance-tech-hackers-push-back/) 和 [digital rights organizations](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/03/meet-rayhunter-new-open-source-tool-eff-detect-cellular-spying) 越來越多地分享了讓人們繞過日常監控的創意方法。

像 FIFA 世界盃這樣的強大科技公司與全球社會政治影響力之間的聯繫，應該受到更多的審視，而不是現在的情況。面對這種權力，那些抵制 AI 驅動監控的抵抗力量所積累的動力，不會隨著哨聲響起而結束。展望即將舉行的 2028 年奧運會和帕運會，社群正團結起來並從 [previous Olympic Games](https://prismreports.org/2024/09/05/los-angeles-olympics-protests/) 中學習，以建立呼籲公司、政府和其他利益相關者投資於人而非監控叢林的活動。

# 在 2026 世界盃的背後：被監視的世界

支持 2026 年世界盃擴展監控工具和執法能力的公司的身影，將成為這次歷史性賽事留下的另一種傳承。美國、墨西哥與加拿大為了確保賽事安全而建立了一個以監控為基礎的生態系統。在過去的男子足球世界盃（南非、巴西及卡達）、巴黎奧運與帕運會中，我們也曾見證過類似的發展。

本週，隱私權排名組織 (Ranking Digital Rights, RDR) 發布了一項深入調查 [1](https://rankingdigitalrights.org/2026/07/14/no-fair-play-mapping-the-2026-world-cup-surveillance-stack/)，揭露了在 2026 年世界盃 16 個主辦城市中，協助建構或強化監控結構的公司。我們發現至少有 21 家公司參與其中，這些公司提供產品與服務，幫助建立並提升用於監控、追蹤及描繪球迷、遊客和當地居民的監控系統。

這些供應商提供的項目被歸類為一個五層堆疊：大規模資料收集、預測性執法、通訊攔截、數據整合以及指揮中心，最後是空中監視。

那麼，「監控堆疊」到底是什麼？我們採用了紐約大學法律教授 [Vincent M. Southerland](https://www.uclalawreview.org/the-masters-tools-and-a-mission-using-community-control-and-oversight-laws-to-resist-and-abolish-police-surveillance-technologies/) 提出的框架：監控堆疊是一套用於「無差別監視」且「罕見受搜索令或傳統法律監督機制約束」的技術集合，指引著關於「何人應被執法、何地執法、如何執法以及何時執法」的決策。這包括 AI 驅動系統處理與分析大量資料以監控、追蹤並描繪個人及社區的能力。

## 2026 世界盃：隱私權挑戰

在2025年7月，美國國土安全部宣布推出一項 [新補助金](https://www.fema.gov/fifa-world-cup-2026)計畫，由聯邦緊急事務管理局（FEMA）主導，撥款846萬美元以加強安保措施並防範無人機威脅，針對美國主辦的11個城市提供支援。雖然這些資金的具體用途及受益企業的詳細說明難以追蹤，但已知亞特蘭大、波士頓與達拉斯將部分補助金用於擴展無人機單位的建置、監視攝影網路以及即時警務情報系統的能力。透過此項計畫或其他補助案取得新合約的公司中，包含如武器科技製造商Axon及技術諮詢巨擘Booz Allen Hamilton等長期合作的政府供應商。

儘管出現這波資金挹注，主辦城市卻未能建立完善的盡職調查程序、風險緩解機制以及處理與監視產品和服務相關的人權影響損害的補救措施。2026年，首次有此項賽事要求每個主辦城市制定自己的人權行動計畫。然而截至今年4月，僅有16個地點中的 [四個](https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/04/10/world-cup-2-months-out-fifa-and-host-cities-sideline-rights) 發布了計畫。根據RDR的報告，當時已有三座城市——西雅圖、墨西哥城與蒙特雷——尚未公開其計畫。（蒙特雷於6月2日將人權行動計畫發布於Instagram，但僅限於限時動態。）

The majority of the action plans did not fully consider the human rights impacts that could arise from the extensive use of technology, especially surveillance and data protection risks. Only Boston, Toronto, and Vancouver had dedicated sections with considerations for the right to privacy. Vancouver was the only city that established a clear and explicit plan for when the technology used during the World Cup—namely the expanded CCTV infrastructure—would be dismantled.

The omissions in the host cities’ human rights action plans are the latest chapter in the history of opacity and lack of accountability over surveillance and policing, particularly in the US. Companies like Flock Safety, Clearview AI, and Palantir are already established providers of tech used by law enforcement agencies at various jurisdictional levels. But the municipal action plans display a complete lack of recognition for how existing surveillance infrastructure could impact the rights of locals and fans. For example, in Atlanta—one of the [most surveilled cities](https://www.acluga.org/issues/speech-and-privacy/) in the US—law enforcement has used Flock Safety‘s license plate reader cameras to conduct immigration lookups on behalf of ICE. In Kansas City, the municipal Transportation Authority plans to install facial recognition cameras in public buses after delaying their deployment during the tournament, prompting fears among civil rights advocates that the technology will continue to operate indefinitely.
